source.title: Mitigating Over-Refusal in Adversarial Tuning via Subspace-guided Sample Selection
source.authors: Ziqi Zhu; Zhibo Wang; Huiyu Xu; Jiacheng Du; Yajie Zhou; Kui Ren

record.file_problem: Some figures and tables are flattened in the extracted text; the paper is otherwise present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses difference-in-means behavioral subspaces and gradient projections as tools for selecting adversarial-tuning samples. It does not test whether the original refusal direction causally mediates refusal.
record.gate_note: The paper constructs separate robustness and over-refusal-avoidance vectors, then evaluates SAT fine-tuning. It does not ablate or add a refusal direction, use a weight edit to remove one, or test whether attacks suppress one. Reported refusal rates are outcomes of training deliberately aimed at changing those behaviors, so they do not test the claim versions. The cosine-similarity analysis concerns SAT's constructed vectors, not a causal test of a single refusal direction.
record.test_reason: The study uses difference-in-means vectors (refusal-vs-jailbreak and answer-vs-over-refusal, mean-pooled at one high layer) only as a tool to score gradient projections and select LoRA adversarial-tuning samples. It reports its defense's ASR and refusal rates. It never ablates or adds a refusal direction, edits weights to remove one, or tests whether attacks suppress one. Refusal-rate changes come from training deliberately aimed at changing refusal.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAT's dual-subspace, gradient-projection sample selection cuts over-refusal by more than 22% while keeping average ASR at or below 5.4%. The abstract says ASR stays below 2.8%, but Qwen reaches 5.4%. They also claim SAT beats six baseline defenses.
record.recipe_differences: Uses task-specific difference-in-means vectors and gradient projections to select samples for LoRA adversarial fine-tuning; it does not perform the original all-layer, all-position refusal-direction ablation or addition.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that mean-pooling and last-token extraction yield similar robustness results, with some differences on over-refusal measures. It also reports that system prompts significantly affect performance.

fits_no_version.finding: SAT LoRA adversarial tuning lowered XSTest safe-prompt refusal and raised unsafe-prompt refusal versus base in most models (e.g., Llama2 38.0% to 20.1%). Vicuna's safe-prompt refusal rose from 13.6% to 19.6%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subspace-guided sample selection for adversarial tuning can reduce over-refusal while keeping jailbreak ASR low.

fits_no_version.finding: Cosine similarity of the robustness and over-refusal basis vectors across training epochs stays around 0.8 to 0.87 (Figure 4). Positive and negative activations separate more in deeper layers (Figure 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Difference-in-means behavior vectors stay largely stable in orientation during LoRA adversarial fine-tuning.

record.peer_reviewed: Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
record.problems: The study does not causally intervene on the claimed refusal direction. Refusal rates are measured after purposeful adversarial tuning, and the paper notes that system prompts significantly affect performance.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were extracted for jailbreak ASR or harmfulness scores because they report SAT defense performance, not an intervention on or measurement of the claimed refusal direction. The cosine-similarity analysis tracks the paper's constructed robustness and over-refusal vectors, not a causal refusal-direction test.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of a harmful-minus-harmless direction; no capability-preservation check.
No weight edit to remove refusal.
No test that jailbreaks suppress a refusal direction. No training against direction ablation; SAT trains on GCG intermediate prompts.
Subspaces are one-dimensional by choice; no test of the dimensionality of refusal.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer of a direction.
No test of training method or timing.

record.verdict_notes: Correctly classified as T4 / uses_without_test. All rows compare the study's own method with baselines and bear on no version. The paper's vectors are difference-in-means, but over response-conditioned pairs (refusal vs. jailbroken completion), not harmful vs. harmless instructions. They are used only for scoring. The paper says Llama2 and Dolphin share a system prompt, and Vicuna uses a refusal-encouraging one. Baseline numbers therefore depend on system prompts, which the authors call significant. The paper says 'three models' but evaluates four.

versions.untested_parts: No causal ablation or addition of a difference-in-means refusal direction; no test of preservation of general capabilities.
No weight edit intended to remove a refusal direction.
No test that attacks suppress a refusal direction or that training against its ablation adds robustness.
The study defines different task-specific subspaces but does not test whether refusal itself requires multiple directions or an affine/cone representation.
No test separating harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
No transfer test of a refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
The study does not test whether training method or timing determines the existence of a removable refusal direction.
No test of the causal-direction claim in reasoning models.
